slides: Open by saying that the two-dimensional transformation vocabulary now has a spatial counterpart, but orientation becomes more visible through volume. A motion or similarity in space can preserve all pairwise distances or scale them uniformly while either preserving or reversing handedness.

Use the route slide to organize a chapter that otherwise has many named motions. We first classify direct and opposite isometries by signed volume, then build central inversion from reflections, produce rotations and translations from two planes, study twists, add scale, and finish with sphere-preserving maps.

The orientation slide should make determinant sign tangible. The tetrahedron keeps its pairwise distances under both isometries, so distance tests alone cannot detect handedness. Signed volume and determinant separate the direct frame from the opposite frame with residuals at numerical precision.

Central inversion is opposite in three dimensions because it negates every coordinate direction. The static figure connects the point reflection to three perpendicular plane reflections, and the determinant value negative one records that all three coordinate axes have had their orientation reversed.

Products of two plane reflections give the spatial version of a familiar planar rule. Intersecting mirror planes rotate by twice their angle, while parallel mirror planes translate by twice their gap. The checks show a sixty-four degree rotation and a translation vector of length one point four.

A twist, or screw motion, combines rotation about an axis with translation along that axis. It preserves distances and radial distance from the axis, but it has no fixed point when the axial step is nonzero. The least-squares residual equals the imposed axial step.

Dilative rotation adds similarity scale to the rotational axis picture. The determinant becomes lambda cubed, so positive lambda is direct and negative lambda is opposite in three dimensions. The two sampled cases share the same rotation angle but have opposite orientation behavior.

Sphere preservation is the closing stress test for spatial similarity and inversion. A similarity sends a sphere to a sphere with a predictable center and radius, while inversion in the unit sphere also fits a sphere. The residuals certify these are not just visual approximations.

The classification slide turns the chapter into a practical workflow. First check whether pairwise distances are preserved or uniformly scaled, then inspect determinant sign, then use fixed sets such as axis, plane, point, or none to distinguish rotations, reflections, twists, inversions, and dilative rotations.

Close by tying the visual labs to one invariant vocabulary. Distances identify isometries, ratios identify similarities, determinant sign identifies handedness, products of reflections generate motions, twists add axial translation, and sphere preservation shows that the transformation view extends beyond planes.
